summary: The English of 5:1-5:6 is faithful and follows Bartenura and Rambam throughout; its chief fault is in 5:4, where the edition's parenthesized source reference (במדבר יד) was rendered as part of the mishnah and the grammar note claimed the mishnah cites a chapter. The senses were filled mechanically with '1': many point to the wrong homograph (place and personal names such as Dor, Bajith, Tob, Sacar, Beer, Nahash, Ashan, Shamir; 'ploughshare', 'lamb', 'bird of prey') or to an etymology or placeholder line, and are corrected to the right Jastrow or BDB entry or removed with a note. Several learner notes were false (Nifal for the Nitpael נִתְנַסָּה, 'Aramaic-influenced' תלמוד לומר, 'slaughterers', Bartenura's variant כְּשֶׁאָלִין misread as בְּשֶׁאָלִין, a shared root for נִסִּים and נִסְיוֹנוֹת), and two commentary summaries misreported Bartenura. The model morphology had wrong genders (מַאֲמָר, דּוֹר, נִסָּיוֹן, לוּחַ, בְּאֵר), a false segmentation of בְּשַׂר, unsplit suffixes, missing elided articles, wrong person in אָלִין and וַיְנַסּוּ, and בָּרוּךְ and פְסוּל misanalysed.

patches.value: The midrashic formula מַה תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר, 'what does (Scripture) teach by saying': תַּלְמוּד is 'teaching', לוֹמַר 'to say'. It is Hebrew, not an Aramaism.
patches.reason: The formula מה תלמוד לומר is Hebrew (the Tannaitic midrashic idiom); the note's 'Aramaic-influenced' is not true.

patches.value: Bartenura: one who destroys a work made in one day is not like one who destroys a work made over many days; so the world's being made by ten utterances makes the wicked's destruction of it graver. The English keeps the refrain 'that was created by ten utterances' in both clauses.
patches.reason: Bartenura does not explain the repetition of the refrain; he explains why ten utterances make the destruction graver ('אינו דומה המאבד מלאכה שנעשית ביום אחד למלאכה שנעשית בהרבה ימים').

patches.value: Rambam: these generations are the Torah's genealogies, so-and-so begot so-and-so in order. This list and those after it are mentioned because the ten utterances were mentioned; they hold moral instruction for a person, to rouse him and to perfect his soul in the moral and intellectual virtues, which is the aim of this tractate.
patches.reason: The summary had the ten utterances 'told to a person'; Rambam says the lists (שבהן מוסר לאדם) hold instruction, and that they follow the mention of the ten utterances.

patches.value: Ten miracles were done for our fathers in Egypt, and ten at the sea. Ten plagues the Holy One, blessed be He, brought upon the Egyptians in Egypt, and ten at the sea. With ten trials our fathers tested the Omnipresent, blessed be He, in the wilderness, as it is said (Numbers 14): "They have tested me these ten times, and have not listened to my voice."
patches.reason: '(במדבר יד)' is the printed edition's source reference in parentheses, not the mishnah's words; the English made it part of the sentence ('as it is said in Numbers 14'). It now stands in parentheses.

value: The mishnah has three parallel statements of ten: miracles in Egypt and at the sea, plagues in Egypt and at the sea, trials in the wilderness. The second sentence explains the first.
נִסִּים (miracles, from נסס) and נִסְיוֹנוֹת (trials, from נסה) come from different roots but sound alike; the mishnah plays on the likeness: God's miracles, the people's testing.
In the first two sentences the second 'ten' is elliptical: וַעֲשָׂרָה עַל הַיָּם, 'and ten at the sea', the noun is understood from the first half.
הֵבִיא ... עַל is the idiom 'to bring upon' (a plague); הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא is the subject, separated from the verb.

The proof text is Numbers 14:22, וַיְנַסּוּ אֹתִי זֶה עֶשֶׂר פְּעָמִים, introduced by שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר 'as it is said'. The parenthesized (במדבר יד) is the printed edition's reference, not the mishnah's; Vilna adds the verse number כב.
patches.reason: Two notes were false: the two nouns do not share one root, and the mishnah does not cite a chapter; the reference is editorial.

value: Quotation: Numbers 14:22, וַיְנַסּוּ אֹתִי זֶה עֶשֶׂר פְּעָמִים וְלֹא שָׁמְעוּ בְּקוֹלִי, from the Hebrew of the mishnah.
Variants: 5:4.18 Vilna ועשרה for וְעֶשֶׂר; 5:4.21 Vilna עשר for עֲשָׂרָה; 5:4.34 Vilna אותי for אֹתִי.
Editorial reference: (במדבר יד) after שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר is the edition's, not the mishnah's text; Vilna reads (במדבר יד, כב), adding the verse.
patches.reason: The Vilna variant כב (the verse number of the reference) was not recorded, and the reference was not marked as editorial.

patches.value: Ten miracles were done for our fathers in the Temple. No woman miscarried from the smell of the holy flesh; and the holy flesh never turned putrid; and no fly was seen in the slaughterhouse; and no emission befell the high priest on the Day of Atonement; and the rains did not extinguish the fire of the wood-pile; and the wind did not overcome the column of smoke; and no disqualification was found in the omer, the two loaves, or the showbread; they stood pressed together and bowed with room to spare; and no serpent or scorpion ever harmed anyone in Jerusalem; and no man said to his fellow, "The place is too narrow for me to lodge in Jerusalem."
patches.reason: 'ever' renders מֵעוֹלָם, which the Hebrew has only with the holy flesh and with serpent and scorpion; it was added without a mark to the first and the last items.

value: The mishnah opens with the heading 'ten miracles' and lists ten items. The first begins with לֹא, the others with וְלֹא, 'and not', except the eighth (standing pressed together and bowing with room), which is stated positively, one miracle in two halves.
הִפִּילָה (Hifil of נפל) is literally 'caused to fall'; with אִשָּׁה as the subject the sense is miscarriage. The verb is feminine singular because the subject is.
קֶרִי is the legal term for a seminal emission; the high priest on the Day of Atonement could not be unclean.
עוֹמְדִים צְפוּפִים וּמִשְׁתַּחֲוִים רְוָחִים is a contrast of two participles with adverbial adjectives: the miracle is that they were crowded when standing and spacious when bowing.
The last item quotes direct speech: צַר לִי הַמָּקוֹם, 'the place is too narrow for me', an echo of Isaiah 49:20, where הַמָּקוֹם is not God but the physical place; here the same word is 'the place'.
שֶׁאָלִין is the relative שֶׁ with the Qal imperfect 1st person singular of לין, 'to spend the night, lodge': 'that I should lodge'. Bartenura notes the variant כְּשֶׁאָלִין, 'when I lodge'.
patches.reason: The standing-and-bowing item is the eighth, not the last; and Bartenura's variant is כְּשֶׁאָלִין, not בְּשֶׁאָלִין.

value: Variants: 5:5.24 Vilna אירע for אֵרַע; 5:5.46 Vilna בעומר for בָּעֹמֶר; 5:5.54 Vilna רווחים for רְוָחִים.
Cross-reference: Isaiah 49:20, צַר לִי הַמָּקוֹם גְּשָׁה לִּי וְאֵשֵׁבָה, cited by Bartenura and Rabbeinu Yonah for the idiom.
Bartenura notes the variant reading כְּשֶׁאָלִין ('when I lodge') for שֶׁאָלִין in the last item.
patches.reason: Bartenura writes וְיֵשׁ סְפָרִים שֶׁכָּתוּב בָּהֶן כְּשֶׁאָלִין: the variant is with כ, not ב.

value: The mishnah lists ten created things in an elliptical series of nouns after the heading 'and these are they'; each after the first is joined with וְ-. No verb is repeated.
בֵּין הַשְּׁמָשׁוֹת, literally 'between the suns', is the idiom for twilight; the mishnah means twilight of the first Friday evening, at the close of creation.
וְיֵשׁ אוֹמְרִים, 'and there are those who say', is the mishnaic form for an anonymous alternative opinion; here it adds three further items, then another.
The Hebrew uses שֶׁל ('of') for possession in קְבוּרָתוֹ שֶׁל מֹשֶׁה and אֵילוֹ שֶׁל אַבְרָהָם: the suffix on the noun is doubled by the phrase with שֶׁל.

צְבָת בִּצְבָת עֲשׂוּיָה gives the reason of those who say it: tongs are made with tongs, so the first tongs must have been made by Heaven. Bartenura adds that the Gemara (Pesachim 54) answers that the first could have been cast in a mould.
patches.reason: The first item has no וְ-; and the riddle's conclusion is the opinion of 'some say', which Bartenura reports the Gemara rejects, not a fact.

The English keeps the name 'shamir'.

patches.reason: בָּרוּךְ is the Qal passive participle of ברך, 'blessed'; its lemma is the verb בָּרַךְ, not a noun or adjective בָּרוּךְ (which the lexicon resolves to the name Baruch).
יְנַסּוּ is 3rd person masculine plural (the imperfect distinguishes gender; the feminine is תְּנַסֶּינָה), and the וַ is the consecutive of a wayyiqtol, not a plain conjunction.
בְּשַׂר is the construct of בָּשָׂר; the בּ is the first root letter, not the preposition ב.
בְּשַׂר is the construct of בָּשָׂר; the בּ is the first root letter, not the preposition ב.
אֵרַע (Vilna אירע) is the Piel perfect, with compensatory tsere before ר (Jastrow אָרַע Pi. 'to befall'); the Qal would be אָרַע.
פְסוּל with shewa is the noun 'disqualification, defect', the subject of נִמְצָא; the adjective is פָּסוּל.
The root of שְׁנַיִם / שְׁתַּיִם is שנה (BDB); 'שנ' is not a root.
לֶחֶם is in construct with הַפָּנִים ('bread of the presence'); its construct has the same form as the absolute.
אָלִין, with the prefix א-, is 1st person singular ('that I lodge'); the plural would be נָלִין.
In עֶרֶב שַׁבָּת it is עֶרֶב that is construct; שַׁבָּת is the absolute that ends the chain.
בְּאֵר is feminine (Jastrow: f.; Bartenura בְּאֵרָהּ שֶׁל מִרְיָם ... שֶׁפָּתְחָה פִּיהָ).
מַטֶּה is from נטה (the נ assimilated into the ט); 'מטה' is not its root.

verdicts.comment: Bartenura prefers the literal sense, that the wicked destroy the world itself by tipping it toward guilt; 'who destroy the world' carries it.
'received ... the reward of them all' is his reading.
The miracles in Egypt are Israel's being spared the plagues; 'done for our fathers' agrees.
Bartenura's 'floating' derivation still describes a crowd pressed together; the English is consistent and records the derivation.
'with room to spare' carries his four cubits.
He reads שֶׁאָלִין, as the base text and the English do.
His 'form of the letters' fits the neutral 'the script'; Rambam's reading is recorded.
The English keeps the saying; the grammar note now reports the Gemara's rejection that Bartenura cites.
Rambam: one utterance could have sufficed; the ten show the worth of what the wicked ruin. The English keeps the rhetorical question.
Agrees with Bartenura on the miracles in Egypt; the English agrees.
Rambam's account of the open altar and the court agrees with the English.
